passages.t: If only he knew where to find Him
passages.happening:
‘Then Job answered’ (verse 1). “Even today my complaint is bitter. His hand is heavy despite my groaning. If only I knew where to find Him, so that I could go to His seat” (verses 2-3).

He would lay his case before God and fill his mouth with arguments, and learn how God would answer. “Would He contend with me in His great power? No, He would certainly take note of me. Then an upright man could reason with Him, and I would be delivered forever from my Judge” (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
Job does not answer Eliphaz's charges point by point. He turns from the friends to God, as he did in chapters 9, 13 and 19. The hope for a hearing comes back here in its most personal form. Job's problem is not only that God seems unjust, but that God seems absent.

A plaintiff who wanted justice went to the place where the king or judge sat, set his case in order and presented his arguments. The word for seat in verse 3 means a fixed place or dwelling. Job pictures God's throne as a court where he could be heard, if only he knew the way.

Notice the change from chapter 9. There Job feared that God would crush him with power. Here he hopes that God would listen.

In verse 2 the traditional Hebrew text makes the heavy hand Job's own; the BSB follows the ancient Greek and Syriac translations in making it God's.
passages.asks: Job longed to know where to find God. Ask whether you have felt that longing. And ask what you would say first if you could set your case before him.

passages.t: He knows the way Job takes
passages.happening:
“If I go east, He is not there, and if I go west, I cannot find Him. When He is at work in the north, I cannot behold Him; when He turns to the south, I cannot see Him” (verses 8-9).

“Yet He knows the way I have taken; when He has tested me, I will come forth as gold” (verse 10). Job has kept to God's tracks without turning aside. “I have not departed from the command of His lips; I have treasured the words of His mouth more than my daily bread” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Hebrew described the compass by facing the sunrise. The word for east also means in front, west means behind, north is the left hand and south the right. Job has looked in front of him, behind him, to the left and to the right, and God is nowhere.

The picture in verse 10 comes from refining gold. Ore was heated in a crucible until the impurities separated and pure metal remained. The friends assume that suffering exposes hidden sin. Job believes that his testing will prove him pure. He has not been told about the scene in heaven, yet he reaches a truth the reader already knows: God is not destroying him for sin.

Bread was the staple of the ancient world. To treasure God's words more than daily bread was to value them above survival itself.
passages.later: The Psalms use the same picture of testing: “For You, O God, have tested us; You have refined us like silver” (Psalm 66:10).
passages.hard:
Job says God cannot be found anywhere. How does that fit with the belief that God is everywhere?

The Old Testament teaches that God is present everywhere; Psalm 139 says there is no place one can flee from him. Job does not deny it. In the same breath he says that God knows the way he has taken (verse 10). What he describes is the experience of God's hiddenness: present but silent, near but not reachable for the hearing Job wants.

Many interpreters distinguish between God's presence everywhere and his favorable, revealing presence, the kind known in worship or in answered prayer. The Psalms often lament the hiding of God's face (Psalms 13 and 88, for example). Others stress that Job's words are honest poetry of distress, not a teaching about God, and that the book lets him speak this way without rebuke.

Both readings agree that Scripture takes the experience of God's absence seriously, and that the right response is not to deny it but to bring it to God, as Job does.
passages.asks: Job could not find God, and he trusted that God could find him. Ask whether you can hold both of those at once. And ask what it would mean to treasure God's words even in a season when he seems silent.

passages.t: Terror before the God who does as He pleases
passages.happening:
“But He is unchangeable, and who can oppose Him? He does what He desires. For He carries out His decree against me, and He has many such plans” (verses 13-14).

“Therefore I am terrified in His presence; when I consider this, I fear Him. God has made my heart faint; the Almighty has terrified me. Yet I am not silenced by the darkness, by the thick darkness that covers my face” (verses 15-17).
passages.hearers:
The chapter moves between confidence and dread more quickly than any before it. The God who knows Job's innocence is also the God who does whatever he wills, and Job cannot see his purpose. For Job, God's sovereignty is not a comfort here. It is a weight.

He is unchangeable translates a compact Hebrew phrase, literally something like he is in one, and some translators render it he is one, or he has decided. Verse 17 is also difficult. The BSB reads it as resolve: the darkness has not silenced Job. Other translations read it otherwise.

Even so, the chapter ends with Job still speaking.
passages.later: The Psalms pray from the same darkness: “Why, O LORD, do You reject me? Why do You hide Your face from me?” (Psalm 88:14).
passages.asks: Job was afraid of God and kept speaking to him. Ask whether fear has ever made you go quiet before God. And ask what it would mean, as for Job, not to be silenced by the dark.
